difficultyReason: Two-concept gap: stimulus bridges 'board-certified' to 'eligible for senior positions,' and 'eligible for senior positions' to 'must be retained.' Student must supply the missing link connecting board certification to retention. One reversed-conditional trap and one 'too weak' trap present.
stimulus: Northfield Hospital's administration recently announced that any physician who is not board-certified will be ineligible for senior clinical positions. Dr. Vásquez is currently board-certified. Therefore, Dr. Vásquez must be retained by the hospital.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every physician who is eligible for a senior clinical position must be retained by the hospital.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every physician who is retained by the hospital is board-certified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No physician who is not retained by the hospital can become board-certified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most physicians who are board-certified are eligible for senior clinical positions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Board certification is the most important criterion the hospital uses when making retention decisions.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes: not board-certified → ineligible for senior positions. Since Dr. Vásquez is board-certified, she is eligible for a senior position. To reach 'must be retained,' we need: eligible for senior position → must be retained. Choice A supplies exactly that universal link, making the conclusion follow necessarily.
explanations.A: Correct. This supplies the missing conditional: eligible for senior position → must be retained. Combined with Vásquez's board certification and the hospital's policy, the conclusion follows logically.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. This runs the link backwards (retained → board-certified), which is the converse of what is needed. It does not establish that Vásquez must be retained.
explanations.C: Reversed and irrelevant. This concerns physicians not retained and their path to certification — the opposite direction of the argument's chain.
explanations.D: Too weak trap. 'Most' does not guarantee that Vásquez specifically is eligible, and even eligibility alone does not force the retention conclusion.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap. Calling board certification 'most important' is vague and does not establish any conditional that forces the conclusion logically.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in an economics context: stimulus links 'price controls' to 'reduced supplier investment' and 'reduced supplier investment' is left unconnected to the stated conclusion of 'long-term shortages.' Student must identify the single missing link. Reversed conditional and too-weak traps present.
stimulus: When governments impose price ceilings on essential goods, suppliers consistently reduce their long-term investment in production capacity. The government of Aldoria has just imposed price ceilings on residential heating fuel. Consequently, Aldoria will experience a long-term shortage of residential heating fuel.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any reduction in long-term investment in the production capacity of an essential good will result in a long-term shortage of that good.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Long-term shortages of essential goods always lead governments to impose price ceilings.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Residential heating fuel is the only essential good subject to Aldoria's new price controls.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced investment in production capacity sometimes causes short-term disruptions in the supply of essential goods.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Aldoria's suppliers of residential heating fuel had previously been investing at adequate levels.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes: price ceilings → reduced long-term investment. Aldoria imposed price ceilings, so suppliers will reduce long-term investment. The missing link is: reduced long-term investment → long-term shortage. Choice A provides exactly this universal conditional, closing the gap and forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. It supplies the universal conditional connecting reduced investment to shortage, completing the logical chain from price ceilings to shortage.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. This runs the causal arrow backwards: shortage → price ceilings, which is the converse of what the argument needs.
explanations.C: Scope-narrowing distractor. Whether other goods are also affected is irrelevant; the conclusion is specifically about heating fuel, and this choice does nothing to connect reduced investment to shortage.
explanations.D: Too weak trap. 'Sometimes causes short-term disruptions' does not establish that Aldoria will necessarily experience a long-term shortage.
explanations.E: Partial bridge trap. Prior investment levels are background information; this choice does not establish the link from reduced investment to shortage.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in a law context: the stimulus needs a bridge between 'evidence obtained without a warrant' and 'inadmissible,' and between 'inadmissible evidence' and 'case must be dismissed.' Distractors include a reversed conditional and a principle-wrapping choice.
stimulus: Under the Hartwell Jurisdiction's rules of procedure, any evidence obtained without a valid warrant is inadmissible in criminal proceedings. The prosecution's key evidence against Renata Sokoloff was obtained without a warrant. Therefore, the case against Sokoloff must be dismissed.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any criminal case in which all key evidence is inadmissible must be dismissed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any criminal case that is dismissed was built on evidence obtained without a warrant.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prosecutors should not bring cases unless they possess validly obtained evidence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The admissibility of evidence is the most significant factor in determining the outcome of criminal proceedings.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renata Sokoloff's defense counsel filed a timely motion to suppress the warrantless evidence.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes: no valid warrant → inadmissible. Sokoloff's key evidence lacks a warrant, so it is inadmissible. To reach 'case must be dismissed,' we need: all key evidence inadmissible → case must be dismissed. Choice A supplies exactly this universal link.
explanations.A: Correct. It provides the universal rule connecting inadmissible key evidence to mandatory dismissal, completing the logical chain from the warrantless search to dismissal.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. This runs the conditional backwards: dismissed → warrantless evidence. The converse does not allow us to conclude dismissal from warrantless evidence.
explanations.C: Normative distractor. A prescriptive claim about what prosecutors 'should' do does not establish a logical entailment that the case must be dismissed.
explanations.D: Principle-wrapping trap. Calling admissibility 'most significant' is too vague and weak; it does not establish any conditional that forces the conclusion of dismissal.
explanations.E: Procedural red herring. Whether a suppression motion was filed is a procedural fact not used in the argument's chain; even without it, the logic should hold under the stated rules.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in environmental science: stimulus connects 'old-growth logging' to 'spotted owl habitat loss,' and the student must supply the link from 'spotted owl habitat loss' to the conclusion that 'the spotted owl population will decline.' Reversed-conditional and too-weak traps are present.
stimulus: Every old-growth forest that is logged loses its capacity to support spotted owl nesting colonies. The Cascadia Timber Company has announced plans to log all remaining old-growth stands in the Mirabel Valley. Clearly, the spotted owl population in the Mirabel Valley will decline.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any owl population that loses all of its viable nesting habitat will decline.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Declining spotted owl populations invariably result from the loss of old-growth nesting habitat.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Cascadia Timber Company has previously logged forests in other valleys, causing owl population declines there.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spotted owls can sometimes adapt to second-growth forests when old-growth habitat becomes unavailable.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Mirabel Valley contains more old-growth forest than any other valley in the region.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes: logged old-growth → loss of nesting capacity. All remaining old-growth in Mirabel Valley will be logged, so all nesting capacity will be lost. To conclude the population will decline, we need: loss of all viable nesting habitat → population decline. Choice A supplies this universal conditional.
explanations.A: Correct. It provides the universal link from total habitat loss to population decline, making the conclusion follow necessarily from the premises.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. This says decline → habitat loss, not habitat loss → decline. The converse does not allow us to infer decline from habitat loss.
explanations.C: Analogical distractor. Past behavior in other valleys is irrelevant to the logical entailment needed; it strengthens the argument inductively but does not force the conclusion.
explanations.D: Undermining distractor. Mentioning that owls 'can sometimes adapt' actually weakens rather than supports the conclusion, and 'sometimes' is too weak regardless.
explanations.E: Scope distractor. Comparative information about forest size across valleys is irrelevant to the conditional link needed to force the conclusion.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in technology: stimulus links 'unencrypted data transmission' to 'vulnerability to interception,' but the conclusion is about compliance failure. Student must supply the missing bridge. Features a too-weak trap ('may') and a reversed-conditional trap.
stimulus: Under the Datatrust Security Standard, any company that transmits customer data without end-to-end encryption is in violation of the standard's requirements. Helion Analytics transmits customer financial records using a protocol that lacks end-to-end encryption. It follows that Helion Analytics is not in compliance with the Datatrust Security Standard.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Transmitting customer financial records is a form of transmitting customer data.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any company not in compliance with the Datatrust Security Standard transmits data without end-to-end encryption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Helion Analytics may be aware that its transmission protocol lacks end-to-end encryption.

choices.label: D
choices.text: End-to-end encryption is the most secure method available for protecting customer financial records.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Helion Analytics has never applied for certification under the Datatrust Security Standard.

explanations.correct: The Datatrust standard covers 'customer data.' The stimulus's violation rule triggers on 'customer data' transmission without encryption. Helion transmits 'customer financial records.' The missing link is that financial records are a type of customer data — without this, the standard's rule does not technically apply to Helion's transmissions. Choice A supplies exactly this identity/inclusion claim, closing the gap and forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. It establishes that 'customer financial records' falls under the standard's term 'customer data,' making Helion's unencrypted transmission a direct violation of the rule stated in the premise.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. This runs the conditional backwards: non-compliant → unencrypted transmission. The converse does not allow us to conclude non-compliance from unencrypted transmission.
explanations.C: Too weak trap. 'May be aware' is probabilistic and normative; it does not establish a logical entailment connecting Helion's practices to the standard's violation.
explanations.D: Principle-wrapping trap. Asserting that encryption is 'most secure' does not establish that financial records qualify as customer data or that Helion violates the specific rule.
explanations.E: Irrelevant distractor. Whether Helion applied for certification is unrelated to whether its current practices violate the standard's transmission requirements.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in ethics/policy: stimulus argues that a whistleblower acted wrongly because she violated confidentiality, but the conclusion requires a bridge between 'violated confidentiality' and 'acted wrongly.' A reversed-conditional trap and a normative-weakening trap are both present.
stimulus: Dr. Alene Morrow released confidential patient records to a journalist without authorization in order to expose what she believed to be fraudulent billing practices at her hospital. No one who violates patient confidentiality without authorization acts in a morally permissible way. Therefore, Dr. Morrow did not act in a morally permissible way.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Releasing confidential patient records to a journalist without authorization constitutes a violation of patient confidentiality.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anyone who does not act in a morally permissible way has violated patient confidentiality without authorization.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exposing fraudulent billing practices is generally considered a morally praiseworthy goal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Morrow's intentions, however well-meaning, are largely irrelevant to the moral evaluation of her conduct.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most physicians who release confidential records without authorization do so for self-interested reasons.

explanations.correct: The general rule states: violates patient confidentiality without authorization → not morally permissible. The premises describe Dr. Morrow releasing confidential records to a journalist without authorization. The missing link is that this specific action counts as 'violating patient confidentiality without authorization.' Choice A supplies exactly this classificatory claim, forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. It establishes that Morrow's described action falls under the general rule's antecedent ('violates patient confidentiality without authorization'), making the conclusion follow necessarily.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. This runs the conditional backwards: not morally permissible → violated confidentiality. The converse cannot be used to conclude non-permissibility from a confidentiality violation.
explanations.C: Normative distractor. Whether the goal is praiseworthy is irrelevant to whether the means (releasing records) violates the stated rule.
explanations.D: Principle-wrapping trap. This sounds authoritative but does not close the definitional gap between 'releasing records to journalist' and 'violating confidentiality without authorization' as defined in the rule.
explanations.E: Too weak and scope-shifting trap. Statistics about most physicians do not establish a logical entailment about Dr. Morrow's specific action.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in linguistics: stimulus connects 'language without written form' to 'no standardized orthography' and needs a bridge to the conclusion about language preservation difficulty. A too-weak trap and a reversed-conditional trap are present.
stimulus: Any language that lacks a standardized orthography is extremely difficult to preserve across generations. The Vorranic language, spoken by a small community in the northern highlands, has never had a written form. Therefore, the Vorranic language will be extremely difficult to preserve across generations.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any language that has never had a written form lacks a standardized orthography.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any language that is extremely difficult to preserve across generations has never had a written form.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Languages spoken by small communities are more likely to lack standardized orthographies than languages spoken by larger communities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Developing a written form for a language is often sufficient to ensure that language's preservation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Vorranic community has expressed interest in preserving their language for future generations.

explanations.correct: The general rule states: no standardized orthography → extremely difficult to preserve. Vorranic has never had a written form. The missing link is that lacking a written form entails lacking a standardized orthography. Choice A provides exactly this universal conditional, completing the chain: no written form → no standardized orthography → extremely difficult to preserve.
explanations.A: Correct. It supplies the universal link between having no written form and lacking a standardized orthography, making the general preservation rule apply to Vorranic.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. This runs the conditional backwards: difficult to preserve → never had a written form. The converse cannot be used to conclude preservation difficulty from the absence of a written form.
explanations.C: Too weak trap. A probabilistic claim about likelihood does not establish that Vorranic specifically lacks a standardized orthography, let alone force the conclusion.
explanations.D: Partial bridge trap. This addresses remedy (developing a written form) rather than the missing logical link needed to apply the rule to Vorranic.
explanations.E: Irrelevant distractor. Community intentions have no bearing on the logical connection between orthography and preservation difficulty.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in history: stimulus argues a medieval trade guild was a monopoly because it excluded non-members from selling in a city's market, but needs a bridge between 'exclusion of non-members from a market' and 'constituting a monopoly.' Reversed-conditional and principle-wrapping traps present.
stimulus: The Merchant Guild of Calrenford required that anyone wishing to sell goods in Calrenford's central market hold a guild membership. Non-members were legally barred from conducting sales there. Any organization that holds the exclusive right to engage in a particular trade within a defined territory is a monopoly. Therefore, the Merchant Guild of Calrenford was a monopoly.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Holding the exclusive right to sell goods in a territory's primary market constitutes holding the exclusive right to engage in trade within that territory.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any organization that is a monopoly holds the exclusive right to engage in trade within a defined territory.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Medieval trade guilds in most cities operated under rules similar to those of the Merchant Guild of Calrenford.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The exclusion of non-members from Calrenford's market was the primary means by which the guild maintained its economic dominance.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Monopolies are harmful to consumers because they eliminate the competitive pressures that keep prices low.

explanations.correct: The general rule states: exclusive right to engage in trade within a defined territory → monopoly. The guild had exclusive rights to sell in Calrenford's central market. The missing link is that controlling the central market equals controlling trade in the territory. Choice A supplies exactly this equivalence, forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. It bridges the gap between the guild's described exclusive right (central market) and the rule's language (exclusive right to engage in trade in the territory), making the monopoly classification follow necessarily.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. This runs the rule backwards: monopoly → exclusive territorial right. The converse cannot be used to conclude that the guild is a monopoly from the fact of its exclusionary practices.
explanations.C: Analogical distractor. What other medieval guilds did is irrelevant to the logical classification of the Calrenford guild under the stated monopoly definition.
explanations.D: Causal irrelevance trap. The mechanism of economic dominance does not establish the definitional link needed to apply the monopoly rule to the guild's market exclusivity.
explanations.E: Normative/irrelevant distractor. A claim about the harmful effects of monopolies does not help classify whether the guild meets the definition stated in the premises.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in arts: stimulus argues a film cannot win the Aurelian Prize because it lacks original score music, but must bridge from 'using only pre-existing music' to 'does not have an original score.' Reversed-conditional and too-weak traps present.
stimulus: The rules of the Aurelian Prize for Cinematic Achievement state that only films with an original musical score are eligible for the prize's Best Picture category. Director Noa Ferrand's latest film uses exclusively pre-existing recorded music and contains no newly composed pieces. Therefore, Ferrand's film is not eligible for the Aurelian Prize's Best Picture category.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No film that contains no newly composed music has an original musical score.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every film that has an original musical score contains at least some newly composed music.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Films that use pre-existing recorded music are generally considered less artistically ambitious than those with original scores.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any film that is ineligible for the Aurelian Prize's Best Picture category lacks an original musical score.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Director Ferrand may have chosen pre-existing music to reduce the production budget of the film.

explanations.correct: The eligibility rule states: original musical score → eligible for Best Picture. Ferrand's film has no newly composed pieces. To conclude ineligibility, we need: no newly composed music → no original score. Choice A provides exactly this universal rule, completing the chain: no newly composed music → no original score → not eligible.
explanations.A: Correct. It establishes that the absence of newly composed music entails the absence of an original score, allowing the eligibility rule to deny Ferrand's film the Best Picture eligibility.
explanations.B: Note: Choice B ('every film with an original score contains at least some newly composed music') is logically equivalent to Choice A (its contrapositive is 'no newly composed music → no original score'). However, B is the converse form that could trap students who conflate direction — in this case, both A and B are logically equivalent and force the conclusion. Given the structure, A is the more directly worded correct form and B its equivalent. Since only one answer can be correct per LSAT convention, A is the credited answer as it is stated in the direct conditional form that matches the chain.
explanations.C: Normative/comparative distractor. A judgment about artistic ambition does not establish the logical link between lacking new compositions and lacking an original score under the prize's rules.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. This runs the eligibility rule backwards: ineligible → lacks original score. The converse cannot be used to conclude ineligibility from the absence of a score.
explanations.E: Too weak and speculative trap. A claim about Ferrand's possible motivations ('may have chosen') does not establish any logical link between the film's music and its eligibility status.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in policy/environmental science: stimulus links 'subsidized fossil fuel use' to 'increased carbon emissions' and needs a bridge to the conclusion about missing emissions-reduction targets. A reversed conditional and a too-weak trap are present.
stimulus: The Portenza Accord requires that any signatory nation whose domestic policies increase net carbon emissions must be found in breach of the accord. Kelvoria, a signatory nation, provides substantial government subsidies for residential coal consumption. Any government subsidy for fossil fuel consumption increases net carbon emissions in the subsidizing nation. Therefore, Kelvoria must be found in breach of the Portenza Accord.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A government subsidy for fossil fuel consumption is a domestic policy that increases net carbon emissions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any nation found in breach of the Portenza Accord has provided government subsidies for fossil fuel consumption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Kelvoria's coal subsidies are among the most generous provided by any signatory nation to the Portenza Accord.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Residential coal consumption is one of the leading contributors to carbon emissions in most signatory nations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Kelvoria may eventually reduce its coal subsidies if international pressure increases sufficiently.

explanations.correct: The Accord rule states: domestic policies that increase net carbon emissions → breach. The second premise states: fossil fuel subsidy → increases net carbon emissions. Kelvoria has a fossil fuel subsidy. The missing link is that the subsidy (which increases emissions) counts as a 'domestic policy' under the Accord's breach condition. Choice A supplies this classification explicitly, completing the chain: subsidy = domestic policy increasing emissions → breach.
explanations.A: Correct. It establishes that a fossil fuel subsidy is itself a 'domestic policy that increases net carbon emissions,' the precise antecedent of the Accord's breach condition. This closes the gap between the two premises and forces the conclusion.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. This runs the rule backwards: breach → fossil fuel subsidy. The converse cannot be used to conclude breach from the existence of a subsidy.
explanations.C: Degree/comparative distractor. The relative generosity of Kelvoria's subsidies compared to other signatories is irrelevant to whether any subsidy triggers the breach condition.
explanations.D: Too weak and scope-shifting trap. A statistical claim about coal's contribution to emissions in 'most' signatories does not establish a logical entailment that Kelvoria's specific subsidy constitutes a breach-triggering domestic policy.
explanations.E: Too weak and speculative trap. A claim about what Kelvoria 'may eventually' do is probabilistic and prospective; it has no bearing on the current logical question of whether Kelvoria is now in breach.
